content:
Hello, I am Will Sweet. I am self-taught and broadly interested in algebra and number theory. I have worked through the exercises in Theorem Proving in Lean 4 and completed some modest practice projects, as well as a formalization of Zolotarev's lemma at https://github.com/glassala/zolotarev.

Although I am interested in eventually contributing to Mathlib, I get the impression that at my current level, I and Mathlib alike would be better served by my simply continuing to hit the books and do practice projects. My current goals are to finish Alex Kontorovich's real analysis game and then Mathematics in Lean.

I was motivated to stop lurking and introduce myself because I found the code in my Zolotarev's lemma project a bit oafish compared to the code in the Mathlib source files it was built atop, even with my best efforts at revision. I am eager to learn how to write better Lean from you all here.

Welcome!

Mathlib is a stretch goal mostly because the "coders" there have spent so much time thinking hard and translating math into Lean, that so many things that are second nature are still alien to new people, and so many considerations will never even cross the mind of a beginner. But, if you want, you can end up there. My personal tips:

  • Use AI sparingly or not at all at the start, it will be hard and maybe dry at times, and annoying without much material. But consult TPIL, MIL, ref docs, search zulip, etc, then maybe even ask here. I think all of those whilst longer in duration may serve better for learning than asking an AI.

  • If your goal is indeed mathlib, one way to self learn is to go to the library and peruse various PRs that were closed, their comments, trying to internalise wth is going on. It can be challenging, in a frustrating sense, but here moments of insight and information , is still more than nothing. And such information an AI will struggle to give you for sure.

  • Focus on math you know well, you did not say much about your background, but the context implies you are a math lean user. Reword various examples and parts of proofs from term to tactic mode, use "show_term" , "apply/exact/try?" , semantic lean searches and loogle as much as you can over AI too.

Also if you did not know about it, this one is a bit of a gentler slope, https://hrmacbeth.github.io/math2001/ . I am genuinely impressed that a self-learner of math can follow MIL well.

Thank you for the advice! I did not mention a mathematical background because, to be blunt, I really don't have one outside of self-study. In the course of my formal education I more or less checked out of math after high school algebra.

It was only a few years ago that I discovered an interest in mathematics but I have taken it seriously since then. As such, the math which I know well is undergraduate-level at highest. I read another post earlier which mentioned that most undergraduate-level math of interest to Mathlib is already in Mathlib, so I have adjusted my expectations accordingly.

I agree that AI is especially insidious to a person in my position because someone studying by their lonesome could easily delude themselves into thinking that it is an adequate substitute for a human mentor or teacher. In the past when I have asked LLMs math/Lean questions, I have not retained their answers so well compared to when I fight through problems on my own with a textbook/the docs.

Yea I mean I technically have a math PhD, but from a meaningless university with little merit, so to most here I am probably their "after high school algebra". Nonetheless I am not an academic in math and likely will never be, but I enjoy doing it and Lean, and as the theorem economy continues to fall perhaps such values will be rediscovered more.

It is about consolidation, you are right, in the sense the above process of searching is extremely likely to lead to higher consolidation. But I can also safely and with high confidence tell you, that AI will randomly and egregiously lie, and it isn't that ideal at Lean code either.

It is easier to use as an "expert" as these mistakes are cheap sanity checks for one, but for learning you risk internalising wrong information, and a human can often provide proper auxiliary context and insight voluntarily. AI is made more to be guided in my view and experience, and it is really not amazing at fully taking the reigns for complicated concepts in the presence of no domain knowledge.

In other words you cannot provide full context as to what you don't know and how to best provide insight to yourself, given you don't know what you don't know at all, and hopefully a teaching human does have a good estimation of this and can extend and elaborate properly without further prompting. Which will be hard without knowing what you don't know either (this is besides the fact it will randomly lie and its lean code is really subpar, although often pragmatically sufficient / a good starting point to mostly rework and golf).

Best of luck, feel free to reach out with lean questions, for what its worth. I may not be much, but all those that are "much" are often too busy as a consequence.
